title: Mahapajapati's thanks
hook: the foster mother's song of thanks to the one she raised (Therigatha, Mahapajapati)

segments.voice: Yesterday, grieving mothers heard Patacara ask about a child's road, salla, the arrow of grief. Your line was where he came from. Did you let your mind travel back, before you met someone you've lost? Today, a mother of another kind, and her thanks. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Hero. That's the word she uses, bowing to a man she once fed as a baby. The woman is Mahapajapati Gotami. She was the sister of the Buddha's mother, Maya, and when Maya died, the texts say, she raised the boy as her own. Much later, she has gone forth herself, and her song is in the collection of the sisters. A child thanking a parent is a familiar scene. This song runs the other way. Today, a foster mother says thank you to the one she raised.
screen: `SHE CALLS HIM HERO.` → `MAYA'S SISTER RAISED HIM.` → `THANKS THAT RUN THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Buddha, hero, homage to you, she says, highest of beings, who freed me from suffering, and many other people too. The woman who once held him now bows. Second, the long view. In the poem she says that in lives before this one she has been a mother, a son, a father, a brother, a grandmother, wandering on without seeing how things are. Parent and child, in her telling, are parts played many times, in both directions. Who raised whom depends on where you stand. Third, a gift that goes both ways. In the Majjhima there's a teaching on offerings that begins with Mahapajapati bringing the Buddha new cloth she has made herself. He asks her to give it to the whole community. Ananda speaks up for her. She was your mother's sister, he says, your nurse, the one who fed you with her own milk when your mother died. And Ananda adds that the help ran the other way too: through the Buddha she found refuge and the teaching. The Buddha agrees, and says a debt like that is not easy to repay. Neither debt cancels the other. Fourth, the close of the song. Truly, she says, Maya gave birth to Gotama for the good of many. So she honors her sister too, the mother who didn't live to see any of it. And she says what honoring the Buddhas looks like: disciples together in harmony, energetic, steady in effort. Her thanks don't stay words. They become a picture of people still practicing.
screen: `HOMAGE TO YOU, HERO.` · `MOTHER, SON, FATHER, BROTHER.` · `A CLOTH, AND A DEBT BOTH WAYS.` · `MAYA GAVE BIRTH FOR MANY.` · then, large: `THANKS TO THE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone you raised, or someone who raised you. Settle, and let the breath be easy. Bring one person to mind: a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a teacher, an older brother or sister, or a child who is grown now. Let their face come. Then find one specific thing to thank them for. Not everything. One: a meal, a ride in the rain, a hard conversation they didn't avoid. Hold it for a few breaths. If they're no longer living, thanks can still be spoken in the heart. The bell holds the time.
Mahapajapati's thanks. The foster mother's song to the one she raised: homage to you, hero, who freed me and many others. Today's word.
Your line: thanks to the child. Today, thank someone younger than you for one thing they taught you, out loud if you can. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember Mahapajapati Gotami as the Buddha's foster mother and as the woman whose request, in the Vinaya, opened ordination to women.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. the Buddha's foster mother has brought him cloth she made herself, and he's asked her to give it to the whole community instead. what do you do?
options: say nothing. it isn't your place.
speak up and remind him what she did for him.
take the cloth to the community yourself.
fork.reveal: Ananda reminds him she was his nurse and fed him when his mother died, and adds that she found refuge through him. the Buddha agrees: the debt runs both ways.

original.note: Pali namo: homage. Mahapajapati's song opens with homage to the Buddha she once raised.

trapdoor: what you thought: a proud mother praising her son.
what it means: a foster mother bows to the one she raised, thanks him for freeing her and many others, and thanks her sister for giving birth to him.
what a scholar hears: the Majjhima's teaching on offerings has Ananda say she nursed him after his mother died; in the Vinaya's Cullavagga, it is her request that opens ordination to women.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 142 (Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta, the teaching on offerings)

notes: All texts are paraphrased; no translation quoted.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 6.6: 'Buddha, hero, homage to you, highest of all beings', freed 'me and many other people'; past roles of mother, son, father, brother, grandmother; disciples in harmony and energetic as homage to the Buddhas; Maya gave birth to Gotama for the sake of many.

MN 142: confirm that she offers a pair of cloths she made herself, that the Buddha asks her to give it to the Sangha, that Ananda intercedes (mother's sister, nurse, foster mother, gave him milk when his mother died), and that the Buddha replies she too was helped by him through refuge and the teaching.
No ages or dates are given for Mahapajapati; the script says only 'much later'.
howItsDone: 'nuns in several traditions honor her as the founder of their order' is a general claim; confirm or soften.

Editor pass: 'she thanks her sister' softened to 'honors' (the verse says Maya gave birth for the good of many, not an explicit thanks); howItsDone's unsourced 'nuns in several traditions honor her as founder' cut; hook closing line varied.

Audit: MN 142 attribution corrected. It is Ananda who says the help ran both ways (she nursed him; through him she went for refuge); the Buddha affirms and says such a debt is not easily repaid. The script had put Ananda's second point in the Buddha's mouth. Teach, myth reveal and fork reveal fixed.
